chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Mithammi, from his two brothers, Muhammad and Ahmad, from Ali ibn Yaqoub al-Hashimi, from Marwan ibn Muslim, from Saeed ibn Amr al-Ju'fi, from a man from the people of Egypt, who said:

My brother bequeathed to me a slave girl who was a singer for him, a luxury, and made her a gift (hadya) to the Sacred House of Allah. So I arrived in Mecca and asked, and it was said to me, 'Hand her over to the Banu Shayba,' and other words were said to me, so there was conflict regarding it. A man from the people of the Masjid said to me, 'Shall I guide you to one who will guide you to the truth in this?' I said, 'Yes.'

He said, 'So he pointed to an old man sitting in the Masjid and said, 'This is Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him), so ask him.' I said, 'So I went to him (peace be upon him) and asked him, and related the story to him.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'Indeed, the Ka'bah neither eats nor drinks, and whatever is gifted to it is for its visitors. Sell the slave girl, and stand on the Hajar al-Aswad and call out: Is there one who has been cut off (by bandits), and is there one who is needy among its visitors? When they come to you, ask about them, give to them, and distribute her price among them.'

He said, 'So I said to him, 'Some of those I asked instructed me to hand her over to the Banu Shayba.' He said, 'But, our Qaim (the Imam), if he had risen, would have seized them, cut off their hands, circled with them, and said: These are the thieves of Allah.'

key_terms.بَنِي شَيْبَةَ: The Banu Shayba clan, custodians of the Ka'bah
key_terms.هَدْياً: Gift or offering, specifically for the Ka'bah

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on gifts given to the Ka'bah and who receives them?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the jurisprudential principle that gifts dedicated to the Ka'bah (hadya) are not consumed by the structure itself but belong to its visitors (zuhhur), specifically the needy pilgrims. Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) illustrates this by instructing the sale of a gifted slave girl and distributing the proceeds, while also contrasting the current custodians' management with the future authority of the Qaim, who will hold the Banu Shayba accountable for their stewardship. This narrative underscores the Shia view of the Ka'bah as a center for social welfare and divine justice rather than a static religious monument.
